summary.title: Efficient and Flexible Integration of Variant Characteristics in Rare Variant Association Studies Using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation
summary.authors: Hana Susak; Laura Serra-Saurina; Raquel Rabionet Janssen; Laura Domènech; Mattia Bosio; Francesc Muyas; Xavier Estivill; Georgia Escaramís; Stephan Ossowski
summary.executive_summary: Rare variant association studies (RVAS) often lack power in small-to-medium cohorts, particularly when genetic variants explain a small fraction of phenotypic variance. Existing methods struggle to integrate individual variant characteristics efficiently without prohibitive computational costs. This study introduces BATI, a Bayesian rare variant Association Test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). Unlike Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approaches, INLA provides rapid, non-sampling-based inference, allowing for the full estimation of complex hierarchical models that incorporate variant-specific covariates. The authors developed 'rvGWAS', a comprehensive framework integrating BATI with five existing tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR) for whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing data. Using semi-synthetic cohorts derived from real Whole-Exome Sequencing (WES) data, the study benchmarks these methods. Results demonstrate that BATI substantially outperforms established tests, achieving power above 75% in scenarios where competitors fail, specifically when risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. The study also identifies eight candidate predisposition genes in a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia analysis, including EHMT2 and COPS7A, validating the framework's utility in real-world applications.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Rare variant association studies (RVAS) often lack power in small-to-medium cohorts, particularly when genetic variants explain a small fraction of phenotypic variance. Existing methods struggle to integrate individual variant characteristics efficiently without prohibitive computational costs. This study introduces BATI, a Bayesian rare variant Association Test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). Unlike Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approaches, INLA provides rapid, non-sampling-based inference, allowing for the full estimation of complex hierarchical models that incorporate variant-specific covariates. The authors developed 'rvGWAS', a comprehensive framework integrating BATI with five existing tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR) for whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing data. Using semi-synthetic cohorts derived from real Whole-Exome Sequencing (WES) data, the study benchmarks these methods. Results demonstrate that BATI substantially outperforms established tests, achieving power above 75% in scenarios where competitors fail, specifically when risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. The study also identifies eight candidate predisposition genes in a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia analysis, including EHMT2 and COPS7A, validating the framework's utility in real-world applications.

Research Context
Rare variants play an important role in complex diseases. RVAS lack power when cohorts are small to medium-sized. Traditional methods struggle with low variance explained. Existing tests often fail to identify risk genes. Current methods lack flexibility in integrating variant features.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a Bayesian test using INLA improve RVAS power? Does integrating variant characteristics increase detection? Will INLA be faster than MCMC for genome-wide scans? Can BATI detect genes explaining <0.5% variance? Does rvGWAS support flexible biological unit analysis?

Methodological Details
Study used realistic semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing cohorts. Simulator combined thousands of real WES datasets. ClinVar risk variants were introduced into VCF files. 1000GP cohort split half samples as cases. Iberian cohort selected one third as cases. Five existing RVAS tests were integrated into rvGWAS. BATI was integrated alongside Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC. HBMR and MiST were also included in the framework. Quality control and filtering are essential functionalities. Analysis was performed on Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study.

Procedures And Architectures
BATI uses Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation for inference. R-INLA package version 17.06.20 was implemented. Model assumes phenotype belongs to an exponential family. Null hypothesis assumes no genetic effects. Alternative hypothesis assumes genetic effect on phenotype. Deviance Information Criteria (DIC) is used for model selection. Difference in DIC (ΔDIC) compares H0 and H1 models. Threshold estimation used S=10 randomly shuffled datasets. BATI integrates categorical and numeric variant characteristics. Full model estimation is performed efficiently.

Key Results
BATI achieves power above 75% in low variance scenarios. Competing tests fail when variants explain <0.5% variance. BATI power reaches close to 100% for three genes. Median power of BATI was 55% at 0.5% VE. BATI calls most genes at 0.01% TIER. BATI shows >80% power at 0.1% TIER. Burden, KBAC, SKAT-O recurrently fail to call BRCA2. HBMR fails to call BARD1, CHEK2, PALB2. Eight candidate predisposition genes were identified. EHMT2 and COPS7A were identified as candidates.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
BATI leverages both categorical and numerical characteristics. Power gains are significant when LoF variants dominate. INLA is substantially faster than MCMC. INLA is more accurate than MCMC given same resources. BATI represents a flexible testing approach. Integration of covariates enhances detection capability.

Contradictions And Limitations
MiST performed poorly on realistic WES cohorts. MiST failed to identify any risk gene at low VE. Burden, KBAC, SKAT-O fail at 0.5% VE. Simulated data lacks complexity of real data. Random causal variants hamper benchmarking of characteristic methods. Small cohort size affects most tests performance.

Claims
BATI outperforms existing RVAS methods on realistic cohorts. BATI achieves power above 75% in low variance. BATI calls most genes at 0.01% TIER. BATI outperforms established RVAS methods. MiST failed to identify any risk gene. Burden, KBAC, SKAT-O fail at 0.5% VE. BATI represents a flexible testing approach. BATI can be further extended and enhanced.
Semi-synthetic cohorts provide more realistic benchmarks than pure simulations. Simulated data lacks complexity and noise-level. Real WES cohorts represent realistic background noise. Pure simulations result in overly optimistic benchmarks. Previous studies relied on pure simulations. Realistic benchmarks reveal profound differences.

Data And Code Availability
rvGWAS supports analysis of whole-exome or whole genome.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
BATI performance is stable despite smaller cohort size. Thresholds were estimated from 10 random splits. S=10 datasets used for robust threshold estimation.

Ethical Considerations
ClinVar risk variants were queried for breast cancer.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 shows gene-wise power plots. Supplementary S6 Fig shows significance thresholds. Table 1 and Supplementary S4 Table used. Supplementary S8 Fig shows Iberian cohort results. Supplementary S9 Fig shows Iberian power plots.

Three Takeaways
BATI integrates variant characteristics efficiently. BATI achieves high power in low variance scenarios. rvGWAS provides a comprehensive analysis framework.
